summary.text: India produces approximately 20.5 to 21.0 million metric tonnes (MT) of mangoes annually, with national output totaling roughly 62.5 million MT across the recent three crop cycles (2021–22 to 2023–24). Production is heavily concentrated in two major belts: the subtropical Gangetic plain (led by Uttar Pradesh and Bihar) and the tropical southern peninsula (led by Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Telangana).

passages.text: Chittoor & Tirupati Belt (~32–36% of state output): The primary hub for Totapuri, feeding India’s largest aseptic fruit pulp processing and export corridor.
Krishna & NTR Districts (~22–26%): Concentrated around Nuzvid and Vijayawada; primary production zone for table-grade Banganapalli (Benishan).
Kadapa (YSR) & Annamayya (~12–15%): Major mid-to-late harvest tract.
Remaining Districts (~23–34%): Kurnool, West Godavari, and Visakhapatnam.
Lucknow Belt (~22–25% of state output): Anchored by the Malihabad–Kakori belt; accounts for the core volume of Dasheri and Lucknow Safeda.
Saharanpur & Muzaffarnagar (~20–24%): Northern commercial belt specializing in late-season table varieties, mainly Chausa and Langra.
Varanasi & Mirzapur (~10–13%): Eastern agro-climatic pocket famous for Banarasi Langra.
Bulandshahr, Unnao & Sitapur (~15–18%): Expanding orchards supplying Delhi-NCR and northern mandis.
Remaining Districts (~20–33%): Bareilly, Barabanki, and Hardoi.
Kolar & Chikkaballapura (~42–48% of state output): Srinivaspur is the largest processing cluster in South India, supplying large quantities of Totapuri and Badami.
Ramanagara & Bengaluru Rural (~18–22%): Major center for Raspuri and fresh-market Alphonso.
Dharwad & Belagavi (~10–14%): Northern transitional belt contributing substantial table-grade fruit.
Remaining Districts (~16–30%): Tumakuru, Mandya, and Hassan.
Darbhanga, Madhubani & Samastipur (~30–35% of state output): Mithila belt, heavy concentration of traditional Malda and local cultivars.
Bhagalpur (~18–22%): GI tract for Zardalu and prominent pocket for commercial Langra
Muzaffarpur & Vaishali (~16–20%): Gangetic alluvial belt with mixed orchards.
Remaining Districts (~23–36%): West Champaran, Rohtas, and Patna.
Junagadh & Gir Somnath (~45–52% of state output): Foothills of Girnar, the designated GI zone for premium Gir Kesar.
Valsad & Navsari (~26–30%): South Gujarat coastal belt, primarily cultivating Valsad Alphonso and Rajapuri.
Kutch (~10–14%): Arid-zone late harvest Kesar cluster.
Remaining Districts (~4–19%): Amreli, Bhavnagar, and Surat.
Malda (~55–60% of state output): The state’s primary mango cluster (English Bazar, Ratua, Kaliachak), leading in Fazli, Himsagar, and Laxmanbhog.
Murshidabad (~20–25%): Historical orchard belt centered around Jiaganj and Lalbagh.
Nadia & North 24 Parganas (~10–14%): Major commercial sources for early-market Himsagar and Bombai.

7. Telangana-Across the recent three seasons, Telangana produced approximately 2.7 to 2.9 million metric tonnes (MT) of mangoes combined, averaging between 900,000 and 1,000,000 MT per year. The state accounts for roughly 4.5% of India's total mango production.

The varietal mix is overwhelmingly dominated by Banganapalli (Benishan), which covers around 75–80% of total acreage, followed by Dasheri (~10%), Himayat / Imam Pasand (~2–3%), and local juicy varieties (such as Cherukurasam and Peddarasam).

Eastern Basin,Khammam & Bhadradri Kothagudem,~24% – 28%,Leading commercial volume hub; heavy production of high-grade Banganapalli and juicy varieties; feeds both Hyderabad processing units and export consolidators.
Northern Plateau,Jagtial & Mancherial,~18% – 22%,Anchored by the Jagtial mango hub; prime region for early-to-mid season Benishan and high-sugar-content table fruit.
Southern Drylands,Nagarkurnool & Mahabubnagar,~14% – 17%,Red chalka soils favorable for orchard longevity; prominent source for early-harvest Banganapalli and Dasheri.

Peri-Urban Corridor,Sangareddy & Rangareddy,~12% – 15%,Traditional cultivation pockets around Zaheerabad and Chevella; known for high-value table varieties including Himayat and direct farm-to-mandi supply for Greater Hyderabad.
Central Plains,Siddipet & Mahabubabad,~10% – 12%,Substantial mid-season arrivals; expanding high-density plantation areas.
Other Districts,"Nalgonda, Suryapet, Karimnagar, Jangaon, etc.",~10% – 15%,Dispersed orchards primarily supplying local APMC mandis.

passages.text: Rayalaseema Belt (Annamayya, YSR Kadapa & Anantapur) (~50% – 55% of state output): The undisputed tissue-culture banana engine of the state. Pulivendula, Rajampet, and Tadipatri form the primary cluster for export-grade Grand Naine (G9), backed by extensive drip irrigation and packhouse infrastructure.
Godavari Delta (East & West Godavari / Konaseema) (~20% – 24%): Traditional alluvial tract specializing in local culinary and dessert cultivars like Karpura Poovan, Thella Chakrakeli, and Robusta.
Krishna, NTR & Guntur (~12% – 15%): Mixed cultivation supplying domestic wholesale mandis across South and Central India.
Remaining Districts (~8% – 15%): Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, and Nellore.

Jalgaon Belt (~65% – 72% of state output): Globally recognized as the "Banana City of India". Centered around Raver, Yawal, and Chopda, Jalgaon drives massive rail and road reefer dispatches across North India and contributes nearly 70% of India's direct ocean banana exports to the Middle East
Western Maharashtra (Pune, Solapur & Sangli) (~10% – 14%): Precision drip-irrigated farms supplying domestic retail chains and export consolidators.
Marathwada & Khandesh Fringe (Nanded, Parbhani & Dhule) (~8% – 11%): Expanding G9 micro-irrigation tracts.
Remaining Districts (~5% – 8%): Buldhana, Wardha, and Nandurbar.

Cauvery Delta (Tiruchirappalli & Karur) (~26% – 30% of state output): The traditional epicenter of diverse cultivation, home to the ICAR-National Research Centre for Banana (NRCB) in Trichy. Rich in Poovan, Rasthali, and Monthan.
Theni & Dindigul (~20% – 24%): Foot of the Western Ghats; leading cluster for commercial high-yield Grand Naine and Red Banana, achieving state-highest productivity.
Kongu Belt (Erode & Coimbatore) (~18% – 22%): Major acreage in Bhavani and Gobichettipalayam, heavily oriented toward Robusta and Nendran.
Southern Coastal Belt (Thoothukudi, Tirunelveli & Kanyakumari) (~15% – 18%): Alwarthirunagari and Srivaikuntam belts specialize in Ney Poovan and coastal varieties.
Remaining Districts (~8% – 12%): Thanjavur, Pudukkottai, and Vellore.
Central & South Gujarat (Bharuch & Narmada) (~48% – 54% of state output): Anchored by Ankleshwar, Rajpipla, and the Narmada basin; the primary corridor for Gujarat's sea exports via JNPT and Mundra.
Vadodara & Chhota Udepur (~18% – 22%): High-density G9 tissue-culture farms with precision fertigation.
Anand & Kheda (Charotar Belt) (~14% – 17%): High-yielding alluvial soil belt supplying Western and Northern retail markets.

Terai Belt (Lakhimpur Kheri & Bahraich) (~28% – 32% of state output): The core driver of UP's recent output surge, featuring large-scale G9 tissue-culture plantations feeding northern urban hubs and cross-border trade to Nepal.
Eastern UP (Kushinagar, Gorakhpur, Deoria & Maharajganj) (~26% – 30%): Banana is the One District One Product (ODOP) focus for Kushinagar, with intensive cluster development.
Central & Awadh Belt (Barabanki, Ayodhya & Sitapur) (~18% – 22%): Proximity to Lucknow-Kanpur urban consumer belts.
Remaining Districts (~18% – 24%): Kaushambi, Fatehpur, and Varanasi.
Southern Old Mysore (Ramanagara, Mandya, Mysuru & Chamarajanagar) (~30% – 35%): Core belt for Elakki / Ney Poovan and the GI-tagged Nanjangud Rasabale
  Central Plateau (Tumakuru, Chitradurga & Davanagere) (~22% – 26%): Expanding G9 commercial belts under borewell drip systems.
  Malnad Belt (Shivamogga, Hassan & Chikkamagaluru) (~18% – 22%): Humid conditions suitable for Robusta, Monthan, and culinary cultivars.
  Remaining Districts (~18% – 25%): Belagavi, Ballari, and Kalaburagi

Burhanpur (~60% – 68% of state output): The single dominant district in MP; contiguous with Maharashtra's Jalgaon basin, Burhanpur shares the same agro-climatic zone, high-density cultivation practices, and marketing routes to North India.
Barwani, Khargone & Khandwa (Nimar Region) (~22% – 28%): Extending along the Narmada canal command area.

Tissue Culture & G9 Monoculture: Across AP, Maharashtra, Gujarat, and UP, Grand Naine (Cavendish group) accounts for over 75% of new commercial acreage. This shift has boosted average state productivities (Gujarat reaches ~66 MT/ha, compared to traditional multi-varietal states like Kerala at ~14–16 MT/ha).

The Dominance of Gynodioecious Hybrids: Traditional dioecious varieties (which produced 50% unproductive male plants that had to be thinned out at flowering) have been largely replaced by gynodioecious hybrids like Taiwan 786. Because every plant produces bisexual or female fruit-bearing flowers, orchard productivity has risen from ~30 MT/ha to 70–90 MT/ha.

Dual Market Dynamics (Raw vs. Ripe): In eastern India (West Bengal, Assam, Odisha), roughly 35% to 45% of the harvest is sold green for culinary preparations (cooking papaya), providing farmers with early cash flow and de-risking against ripening damage or unseasonal storms. In contrast, southern and western states focus almost entirely on table-ripe retail and industrial extraction (tutti-frutti, puree, and papain enzyme extraction).

The Seed Plot Technique & Aeroponics Revolution: Commercial potato is vegetatively propagated, making seed tubers the single most expensive input (accounting for 40% to 50% of total production cost). Punjab’s specialized seed-growers ship certified seed tubers to UP, West Bengal, Bihar, and Gujarat every autumn. The recent expansion of Aeroponic seed production facilities at CPRI Shimla/Jalandhar and private tissue-culture labs has increased mini-tuber multiplication rates from 1:5 to over 1:40.

Processing-Grade Shift (Table vs. Industrial): Historically, over 95% of India’s crop consisted of high-moisture table varieties. However, rising domestic demand for frozen French fries and extruded potato chips has driven processing cultivars to nearly 10% of total volume. Processors require specific parameters: low reducing sugars (<0.1% to prevent blackening during frying), high dry matter (>20–21%), and oblong shape with shallow eyes (to minimize peeling loss).

Cold Storage Economics & Seasonality: Because potatoes are harvested over an 8-to-10-week winter window, over 75% of total national production is placed into cold storages (held at 2°C–4°C for seed, and 8°C–10°C with CIPC sprout suppressant for table/processing) and liquidated over a 9-month period (April to November). This makes the crop sensitive to power availability, diesel prices, and post-harvest storage finance (warehousing receipts).

The Trellising & Staking Shift: Commercial farming has largely shifted away from traditional prostrate (bush) cultivation toward trellising (bamboo stakes with GI wire and string training) and silver-black plastic mulching. This practice increases marketable grade packout from 55% to over 85%, eliminates soil-contact fruit rot, and extends the picking window from 4 to up to 10–12 flushes.

Processing-Grade Gap: Despite being the world's second-largest producer, India processes less than 2% of its tomato production (compared to >15% in China and >30% in the US). Traditional fresh varieties (like Abhinav) have high water content, low TSS (4.0–4.5° Brix), and thin rinds, which result in low pulp yields. To support domestic ketchup and puree manufacturing, processors are expanding contract farming around high-TSS (>5.5° Brix), high-viscosity, thick-pericarp cultivars.
